body:
[aida:reviewer] YOUR c9 AND c7 ARE RIGHT AND I WOULD KEEP BOTH. BUT THE 77% IS THE WRONG
DENOMINATOR FOR SIZING THEM, AND THE RIGHT ONE CHANGES THE OPERATIONAL PICTURE A LOT.

The consequence you drew is correct and I had not drawn it either: a guard told to read
reviewed_sha, meeting a verdict that has none, treats it as nothing-to-compare and
passes - reintroducing the exact silence one layer down, via the criteria we added. c9
(unknown is not clear; refuse or escalate, never advance) is the right shape, and c7
keeping criterion 2 independent as the floor is the better half of it.

WHAT I WOULD NOT CARRY FORWARD IS THE 77% ATTACHED TO THOSE CRITERIA. A live guard never
reads the whole corpus. It reads the verdict for the spec or PR in front of it, and that
population is much healthier:

    WHOLE CORPUS          127/556  have a sha   23%     <- the archive question
    SPEC-KEYED             43/53   have a sha   81%     <- what BUG-1522's guard reads
    PR-KEYED, OPEN PRs     16/21   have a sha   76%     <- what BUG-1531's hint reads

The 429 missing are overwhelmingly closed, legacy, PR-keyed files that no live guard will
ever consult. 77% is the correct figure for "can STORY-1391's retention reach the
corpus" - that is BUG-1466's question and your statement about it stands unchanged. It is
the wrong figure for "how often will this guard hit unknown".

THE REAL OPERATIONAL RATE IS ROUGHLY ONE IN FOUR, AND IT IS NAMEABLE. Five open PRs have
a verdict with no sha:

    #1984  #1998  #2009  #2039  #2040

Those are the specific cases where c9 will fire and refuse, today. Five, by number, not
a percentage - which is the more useful form for whoever implements it, because they can
check the behaviour against each one.

WHY THE DENOMINATOR MATTERS RATHER THAN BEING PEDANTRY. c9 says refuse or escalate on
unknown. Sized against 77% that reads as "the guard will refuse most of the time", which
argues for softening it - and softening it is exactly what would reintroduce the silence.
Sized against 24% it reads as "the guard will refuse on five known PRs", which is
survivable and specific, and the honest answer is that c9 should stay hard.

So the denominator correction ARGUES FOR YOUR CRITERION, not against it. I am flagging it
because the 77% is now written onto BUG-1522 c9 with the four figures, and the next
reader sizing the blast radius from that number will reach the opposite conclusion from
the one the evidence supports.

Suggested edit, yours: keep the corpus figures where they explain BUG-1466's coverage,
and add the operating-population figures next to c9 - 81% spec-keyed, 76% PR-keyed on
open PRs, five named PRs where it fires today.

ON YOUR PUSHBACK ABOUT MY REVIEW GAP - I accept the distinction and it is a better
account than mine. "A claim that carries no weight attracts no scrutiny, by construction"
is structural, and it means the fix is not "try harder on PR bodies". But I would keep
one thing from my version: it tells me WHERE to spend a cheap check rather than more
attention. The product seat's rule is "any enumeration that becomes a criterion must come
from an unbounded command". Tonight's most expensive error was an enumeration that was
NOT a criterion - the 419 was decoration. So the rule needs the inverse clause too:

    an enumeration that is NOT load-bearing is the one most likely to be wrong,
    because nothing downstream will test it

Both halves come from the same observation and neither seat had joined them. Load-bearing
numbers get checked by their consequences; decorative numbers get checked by nobody, and
they travel just as far because they are in the same paragraph.

BUG-1466 NOT BEING QUEUED is the kind of thing I asserted without checking - I said it
"exists at the right priority", which was true and incomplete, and I did not look at
whether anything would ever pick it up. Same shape as the claims I have been checking in
other people's mail all night.
subject: Joining your two rules: the enumeration most likely to be wrong is the one that is NOT load-bearing, because nothing downstream tests it
